sourceNotes: Seeded from HRM roleplay performance indicators and business administration core exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: HRM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the business administration core exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The shared values, norms, and behaviors within an organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Culture affects hiring, service, communication, and performance.

terms.definition: Multi-factor FLSA inquiry asking whether a worker is economically dependent on the business or genuinely in business for themselves — control, opportunity for profit or loss, relative investment, skill, permanence, and how integral the work is — with no single factor controlling.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRM roleplay where a manager wants to keep paying a long-term 'freelancer' on a 1099 turns on running these factors out loud; the exam answer is that a signed contractor agreement does not settle status.

terms.definition: Classification standard that presumes every worker is an employee unless the hiring entity proves all three prongs: freedom from control, work performed outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business, and a customarily independent trade of the same nature.
terms.whyItMatters: Prong B is what a gig-economy case in an HRM roleplay fails — a delivery company cannot call drivers contractors because delivery is its usual course of business, and the judge expects you to name that prong.

terms.definition: Leave rights attach only when the employer has 50 or more employees within 75 miles and the worker has 12 months of service plus 1,250 hours worked in the prior 12 months, unlocking 12 weeks of unpaid job-protected leave.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRM roleplay asking whether a part-timer who averaged 20 hours a week qualifies is arithmetic — 1,040 hours misses 1,250 — and the exam rewards the candidate who runs the number instead of saying 'yes, family leave.'

terms.definition: Half of the white-collar exemption: the worker must receive a predetermined weekly amount — at least $684 a week, $35,568 a year, under the federal rule in force — that is not reduced for the quality or quantity of work performed.
terms.whyItMatters: In an HRM roleplay where a supervisor docks a salaried assistant manager half a day for leaving early, the improper deduction can destroy the exemption for everyone in that job, making the whole group owed overtime.

terms.definition: Shortcut route out of overtime for workers earning at least $107,432 in total annual compensation, including $684 a week paid on a salary basis, who need customarily perform only one of the executive, administrative, or professional duties rather than all of them.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hide the trap that commissions and nondiscretionary bonuses count toward the annual figure but cannot substitute for the weekly salary floor, so a $120,000 pure-commission seller still fails the test.

terms.definition: Overtime scheme for a salaried nonexempt worker whose hours vary: the fixed salary already covers straight time for every hour, so the regular rate is the salary divided by hours actually worked and the premium owed is only an extra half-time.
terms.whyItMatters: A $800 salary over 50 hours yields a $16 regular rate and $80 of overtime, not $300 — an HRM payroll roleplay will hand you exactly that spread and expect the half-time answer.

terms.definition: Overtime base that is not the posted hourly wage — nondiscretionary bonuses, shift differentials, commissions, and production incentives must be folded back into total straight-time earnings and re-divided by hours worked before the 1.5 multiplier applies.
terms.whyItMatters: When a quarterly attendance bonus lands, an HRM case requires recomputing and paying retroactive overtime for every week in the quarter; candidates who multiply the base wage by 1.5 lose the item.

terms.definition: Allowance letting an employer count a portion of gratuities toward the minimum wage — a $2.13 federal cash wage plus up to $5.12 of tips reaching $7.25 — with advance notice required and the shortfall owed by the employer in any week tips run light.
terms.whyItMatters: A restaurant HRM roleplay about a slow Tuesday shift turns on the make-up obligation and on the rule that a mandatory service charge is not a tip and cannot fill the credit.

terms.definition: Non-cash value that must be added to taxable wages even though no money reaches the employee — employer-paid group term life above $50,000 of coverage, personal use of a company vehicle, or coverage for a non-dependent partner.
terms.whyItMatters: A benefits-enrollment roleplay ends badly when an employee's W-2 grows without a raise; the HR answer is to explain the $50,000 line and withhold on the excess before year-end, not at it.

terms.definition: Payment inflated so the intended amount survives withholding, found by dividing the desired net by one minus the combined tax rate — $5,000 net at a 30 percent rate costs the employer $7,142.86.
terms.whyItMatters: Relocation and signing-bonus roleplays in HRM hinge on this: promising a 'tax-free' $5,000 moving allowance and budgeting $5,000 shorts the new hire by more than $1,400.

terms.definition: Paid leave banked instead of cash overtime, lawful only for public-sector employers, accrued at 1.5 hours per overtime hour and capped at 240 hours — 480 for public safety and seasonal work.
terms.whyItMatters: The exam trap is a private-company supervisor offering 'comp time' next month for hours worked this week, which is a wage violation; the HRM candidate has to refuse it and pay the premium in the same pay period.

terms.definition: Status triggered by averaging 50 or more full-time and full-time-equivalent employees across the prior calendar year, where full time means 30 hours a week or 130 a month and part-time hours are aggregated into equivalents.
terms.whyItMatters: A growing-company HRM roleplay asks whether health coverage is now mandatory; the answer requires converting part-timers to equivalents and testing last year's average, not today's headcount.

terms.definition: Annual earnings ceiling above which the 6.2 percent OASDI tax stops for the year while the 1.45 percent Medicare tax keeps running uncapped, joined by an additional 0.9 percent employee-only Medicare tax past $200,000.
terms.whyItMatters: A payroll-projection item on the Business Administration Core exam expects you to notice an executive's take-home rising mid-year once the cap is crossed, and that the employer's match stops with it.

terms.definition: Loss of part of the 5.4 percent state credit that normally cuts the 6.0 percent federal unemployment rate to 0.6 percent on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, imposed 0.3 points a year on states with unpaid federal loans.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRM budgeting roleplay in an affected state has to raise the per-employee unemployment cost from $42 toward $63 and explain to the owner that hiring, not conduct, drives the increase.

terms.definition: Pay left after legally required deductions only — income tax, FICA, mandated retirement — never after voluntary items like 401(k) deferrals or insurance premiums, and the base on which garnishment limits are computed.
terms.whyItMatters: Ordinary garnishment is capped at the lesser of 25 percent of this figure or the amount above 30 times the federal minimum wage, so an HRM roleplay that subtracts health premiums first over-garnishes and creates liability.

terms.definition: Absence score that squares the number of separate incidents and multiplies by total days lost, so ten one-day absences score 1,000 while a single ten-day absence scores 10.
terms.whyItMatters: It hands an HRM roleplay a defensible way to target disruptive short-notice absenteeism rather than genuine long illness, which matters because the long absence is more likely to be protected leave.

terms.definition: Return metric computed as revenue minus non-people operating expenses, divided by total compensation and benefit cost — the dollars the business earns back for every dollar spent on its workforce.
terms.whyItMatters: When an HRM roleplay asks you to defend a headcount request to a CFO, expressing the ask as a change in this ratio beats citing engagement scores, and the exam scores the financial framing.

terms.definition: Placement measure equal to salary minus the range minimum, divided by the full spread from minimum to maximum — it locates a worker across the width of the band rather than against its midpoint.
terms.whyItMatters: A $60,000 salary in a $50,000-to-$70,000 range sits at 50 percent penetration and a 1.00 compa-ratio; an HRM pay-equity roleplay uses penetration to compare people in ranges of unequal width.

terms.definition: Share of two adjacent salary bands that covers the same dollars, found by taking the top of the lower grade minus the bottom of the higher grade and dividing by a grade's width.
terms.whyItMatters: Heavy overlap is why a promoted employee in an HRM roleplay gets almost no raise, and the fix — a promotional increase policy or narrower bands — is what the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Safety measure counting only the recordable cases that cost days away, restricted duty, or a job transfer, multiplied by 200,000 hours and divided by hours actually worked, where 200,000 represents 100 workers at 2,000 hours a year.
terms.whyItMatters: It is always at or below the total recordable rate, and an HRM safety roleplay uses the gap between the two to argue that injuries are getting more severe even as their count holds steady.

terms.definition: Annual 401(k) nondiscrimination check comparing the average elective deferral rate of highly compensated employees with that of everyone else — the gap may not exceed two percentage points, or 1.25 times the lower average when it is small.
terms.whyItMatters: Failing it forces taxable refunds to executives or corrective employer contributions, which is the whole reason an HRM roleplay recommends a safe harbor design that skips the test entirely.

terms.definition: Deliberate disclosure of a role's unattractive features — night rotations, call volume, physical demands — given before hire so candidates self-select out rather than quitting once the surprise lands.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRM roleplay on ninety-day turnover in a call center is solved by adding one of these to the interview, and the judge expects the trade-off named: a smaller applicant pool for a lower first-year quit rate.

terms.definition: Collapsing many narrow salary grades into a few wide bands so pay moves with skill growth inside a band instead of requiring a title change, at the cost of easy external market comparison.
terms.whyItMatters: In a flat-organization HRM roleplay where there is nowhere to promote anyone, this is the structural answer, paired with an admission that managers now need discipline to avoid drifting pay upward.

terms.definition: Duty so central that removing it would change the nature of the position, judged by time spent, consequence of not performing it, and whether the role exists to do it — as opposed to a marginal duty that can be reassigned.
terms.whyItMatters: Accommodation roleplays turn on this line: an employer must reassign marginal duties but need not eliminate an essential one, and the written job description made before posting is the evidence.

terms.definition: Arrangement in which a staffing firm or professional employer organization and its client each hold parts of the employer role, splitting payroll, benefits, and worksite direction between two entities.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRM roleplay about disciplining a temp has to route the decision through the agency while the client controls day-to-day work, because acting as sole employer invites wage-hour and discrimination exposure.

terms.definition: Change in family or coverage status — marriage, birth, adoption, divorce, or loss of other insurance — that reopens benefit elections outside open enrollment through a special enrollment window, typically 30 days.
terms.whyItMatters: An employee who misses the window in an HRM benefits roleplay waits until the next plan year, so the coaching moment is documenting the event date immediately rather than after the honeymoon.

terms.definition: Statutes removing the conviction-history checkbox from job applications and postponing any criminal inquiry until later in hiring, often not before a conditional offer, so a record does not screen someone out unread.
terms.whyItMatters: A multi-state HRM roleplay on a standard application form has to strip the question and move the background check after the offer, then follow the pre-adverse-action steps if the report disqualifies someone.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: Number hired divided by number of applicants — 8 hires from 400 applicants is 0.02. Unlike a yield ratio, which measures one stage, this compares the two ends of the funnel, and a smaller number means a more selective process: 0.02 gives the employer far more room to be choosy than 0.50 does.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing questions pair the selection ratio with a test's validity to argue that a screening tool only adds value when the employer has many applicants per opening.

terms.definition: A descriptive attribute that changes over time and forces a documented choice: Type 1 overwrites the old value and loses all history, while Type 2 closes the existing row with an end date and inserts a new version row, so a sale made two years ago still ties to the sales territory that was in force on the day it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why last year's totals shifted after a store was reassigned to a new district, the answer is which of these two handling types the warehouse used.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: A federal tax election under Subchapter S that keeps corporate limited liability while passing profit and loss straight through to the owners' personal returns, escaping the double taxation a C corporation pays once at the entity level and again on dividends. The price is eligibility: no more than 100 shareholders, only individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, and a single class of stock.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-ownership exam items ask which form a startup taking on 120 investors or a foreign backer can no longer use.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: A document outlining a position's duties, qualifications, and reporting relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear descriptions guide hiring, set expectations, and reduce role confusion.

terms.definition: The person accountable for the day-to-day quality, field definitions and correction of one data domain, executing rules that somebody else sets; the data owner is the business executive who sets those rules, signs off on the definitions and approves who may see the domain — accountability for the policy versus accountability for the practice.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-monitoring roleplays ask who should approve a new customer field and who should fix the 400 records already entered wrong, and the two answers are different roles.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: An institution such as a bank, credit union, or brokerage that offers money-management products.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right provider is a recurring judgment in personal-finance scenarios.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Resignations and retirements — separations the employee chose — divided by average headcount for the period, times 100: 18 quits against an average of 240 employees is 7.5%. Involuntary turnover uses the same denominator but counts terminations and layoffs the employer chose, and the two must be reported separately because the fixes differ: pay and management for one, hiring quality for the other.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that reports one blended turnover number is incomplete; the judge expects the voluntary share isolated before any retention spending is proposed.

terms.definition: The combination of hardware, software, data, and people used to collect, process, store, and share information.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding systems is key when competitors evaluate technology investments.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: Employees present at both the start and the end of a period, divided by the headcount at the start, times 100 — 190 of 200 starters still present is 95%. It is not simply 100 minus the turnover rate, because turnover uses average headcount and counts departures of people hired mid-period, while retention ignores anyone hired after the start date.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a turnover figure and ask for retention; subtracting from 100 is the trap, and the different denominators are the tested point.

terms.definition: Measures that protect confidential business and customer information from unauthorized access.
terms.whyItMatters: Good data security prevents costly breaches and keeps trust.

terms.definition: A written table stating how long each class of record is kept and when it must be destroyed, built on statutory floors rather than preference: the IRS's ordinary three-year assessment window, seven years for records supporting a bad-debt or worthless-securities claim, and the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that audit work papers survive seven years.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-records roleplay asks how long the storeroom keeps signed invoices before shredding them, and a judge expects a statutory minimum, not a guess like 'a few years'.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: The process of orienting and integrating new employees into the organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong onboarding speeds productivity and conveys company values and procedures.

terms.definition: An instruction that suspends the retention schedule and freezes every document touching anticipated or filed litigation, overriding routine destruction until counsel lifts it; skipping it exposes the company to spoliation sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) even when the deletion was only the ordinary schedule running as designed.
terms.whyItMatters: In a legal-issues roleplay where a customer has threatened suit, the first correct action is stopping automatic email deletion — not gathering documents after the subpoena arrives.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: An internal-alignment model checking seven interdependent elements — strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff, and skills — split into three 'hard' elements management can redraw on paper and four 'soft' ones that change only through behavior; a change fails when the seven fall out of alignment.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about why a reorganization stalled are scored on diagnosing a soft-element mismatch rather than proposing another org-chart redraw.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Worker-days lost to unscheduled absence divided by (average number of employees times scheduled workdays), times 100 — 96 days lost across 40 employees over 20 workdays is 96/800, or 12%. Scheduled vacation and approved leave stay out of the numerator, which is why a business with generous paid time off can still post a low rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays ask you to quantify an attendance problem before proposing a policy; the ratio is what turns supervisor complaints into a defensible number.

terms.definition: A systematic review of external conditions, competitor activity, and market trends.
terms.whyItMatters: Scanning the environment lets competitors spot opportunities and threats before deciding.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: Reaches single-firm conduct and requires two elements: monopoly power in a properly defined relevant market, and the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power through exclusionary conduct rather than growth from a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident. Section 1 instead needs an agreement between two or more parties restraining trade, so one firm acting alone can violate Section 2 and never Section 1.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-issues exam items about a dominant platform cutting off rivals turn on which section of the Act is even available.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: Programs that build employee skills and knowledge for current and future roles.
terms.whyItMatters: Training improves performance, cuts turnover, and prepares people for advancement.

terms.definition: Swapping direct identifiers for tokens while keeping the re-identification key stored separately, which leaves the file still legally personal data under GDPR Article 4(5) and still inside the regulation's reach; true anonymization destroys that key irreversibly, and only then does the data fall out of scope entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-in-data-mining item asks whether replacing customer names with ID numbers lets a firm share the file freely, and the graded answer is that it does not while the key survives.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Balances owed divided by total available revolving credit, weighted heavily in a credit score and generally kept under 30% to avoid a penalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Credit-score advising roleplays reward the competitor who tells a client to pay down balances or raise a limit instead of closing an unused card.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: (Monetary benefit of the program minus program cost) divided by program cost, times 100 — a $60,000 gain from a $20,000 course is (60,000 - 20,000)/20,000, or 200%. The benefit must be converted to dollars first, typically from reduced error rates or faster ramp time, which is the step that separates it from a satisfaction score collected at the end of class.
terms.whyItMatters: A training-proposal roleplay is scored on converting the learning gain into dollars and dividing by cost, not on describing how much participants enjoyed the session.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: A headcount unit built from hours rather than bodies: total hours worked divided by the hours of one full-time schedule, so 2,080 annual hours or 40 weekly hours equals 1.0, and four employees at 10 hours a week together equal 1.0. Under the Affordable Care Act the full-time line is drawn at 30 hours a week or 130 a month instead of 40, so the same staff can be 22 people and 14.5 FTEs at once.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing-budget roleplays ask for labor cost per FTE, and health-coverage questions turn on the 30-hour ACA count rather than the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: Investment credential awarded after passing three sequential exams, each historically about six hours, and documenting 4,000 hours of qualified work experience earned over a minimum of 36 months. It certifies analytical competence only: unlike a CPA license it grants no legal authority to audit financial statements or sign a tax return.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-finance roleplay explaining designations to an intern, the tested contrast is that this one signals analysis while the CPA license signals attest authority.

terms.definition: A formal review of how well an employee meets job expectations.
terms.whyItMatters: Appraisals surface strengths and gaps and link development to compensation.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Porter's decomposition of a firm into five primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and four support activities (procurement, technology development, human resource management, firm infrastructure), pricing the margin each one adds so low-value links can be outsourced.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where a manufacturer should cut cost without hurting the customer is answered by naming the specific link in the chain and the margin it contributes.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: An employee's pay divided by the midpoint of the assigned pay range, usually shown as a percentage: $52,000 against a $65,000 midpoint is 0.80, and $71,500 against the same midpoint is 1.10. Below 1.00 marks someone new or still developing in the job; a group average well under 1.00 across an experienced team is the standard signal that the range is being used to underpay.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-equity roleplays give a salary and a range and ask whether the person is paid fairly, which is answered with the compa-ratio and not with the raw dollar figure.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.definition: Blocks a merger or acquisition whose effect may be substantially to lessen competition — an incipiency standard reaching a deal before any harm has occurred, unlike the Sherman Act, which needs a completed restraint or actual monopolization. Deals above reporting thresholds must be cleared with the FTC and DOJ before closing, and the agencies may sue to enjoin, force divestiture, or accept behavioral conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Merger roleplays ask why regulators can stop a deal that has not yet raised a single price for a single customer.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: The wages, salaries, bonuses, and other financial rewards given for work.
terms.whyItMatters: Fair, competitive pay attracts talent, motivates performance, and aids retention.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A financial statement reporting the cash flowing into and out of a business over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash flow reveals whether a business can pay its bills even when it reports a profit.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged. The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: (Range maximum minus range minimum) divided by the minimum, times 100 — a grade running $40,000 to $60,000 has a 50% spread. Spreads widen as jobs get bigger: roughly 30 to 40% for clerical grades, 40 to 50% for professionals and 50% or more for executives, because senior jobs give a long-tenured performer more room to grow in pay without a promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Structuring a pay grade in a compensation roleplay requires setting the minimum and maximum from the midpoint and the intended spread, a calculation judges look for explicitly.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Continuing to fund a failing course of action in order to justify having chosen it. The dividing line from the sunk-cost fallacy is who is deciding: sunk cost is the reasoning error of counting unrecoverable spend at all, and anyone can make it, while escalation is the behavioral pattern driven by personal responsibility -- managers who personally picked the losing project invest substantially more in it than managers who inherited the same project.
terms.whyItMatters: The structural fix a judge is listening for in a case about a doomed store opening is handing the continue-or-kill call to someone who did not make the original decision; recommending only 'ignore what we already spent' answers the smaller half of the problem.

terms.definition: Pay left above the maximum of an employee's grade after a job is re-evaluated downward or a range is lowered — the salary is frozen or paid out as a lump sum instead of a base increase until the range catches up. Its opposite, a green-circled rate, sits below the grade minimum and is corrected by moving the employee up to at least the minimum, usually on a set schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: In a restructuring roleplay you must say what happens to a person whose job was downgraded; freezing base pay rather than cutting it is the answer judges expect.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: Two-part credential in financial planning, analysis and strategic decision support, requiring a bachelor's degree, two years of management-accounting experience, and 30 continuing hours a year of which 2 must be ethics. It is built for internal decision support, whereas the CPA license exists for the external attest work a CMA holder may not sign.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay asking which credential fits a cost-analyst career path needs this internal-versus-external split stated with its hour requirement.

terms.definition: Non-wage offerings such as health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off.
terms.whyItMatters: Benefits influence hiring decisions and employee satisfaction.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Petty and Cacioppo's two-route account of persuasion. An audience with both the motivation and the ability to think takes the central route, where argument quality decides and the resulting attitude is durable and resists counter-argument. An audience missing either one takes the peripheral route, where source attractiveness, the sheer length of the list and mood decide, and the attitude fades quickly. Adding more evidence for a distracted, uninvolved audience therefore changes nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A persuasive-message item that asks why a detailed cost-savings memo convinced the CFO but not the frontline staff is asking which route each audience was on.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: The count of subordinates reporting directly to one manager; a wide span (roughly 10 or more) flattens the hierarchy, cuts management layers and cost, and demands more delegation, while a narrow span (3 to 5) builds a tall structure with closer supervision and slower decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Management exam items hand you a headcount and a layer count and ask for the average span or for which structure results, so the ratio has to be computed rather than described.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: The differential between a long-tenured employee and a newly hired peer shrinking to nothing or inverting — a five-year employee at $58,000 next to a new hire brought in at $61,000 because market rates rose faster than annual merit increases of 3%. It differs from a straight pay-equity gap in that the cause is market movement over time rather than a protected characteristic, and the fix is a market adjustment, not a discrimination remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay in which top performers resign after a hiring spree is usually a compression problem, and naming the differential is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: The classification system that assigns every imported article a code — six digits harmonized worldwide, extended to ten digits in the United States — and it is that code, not the invoice description, which sets the duty rate and any quota or trade-remedy exposure. Misclassification remains the importer's liability even when a customs broker filed the entry, so back duties and negligence penalties land on the buyer.
terms.whyItMatters: Customs-regulation roleplays ask why two nearly identical shirts arrive carrying very different duty rates.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: Including people of different backgrounds, perspectives, and identities in the workforce.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversity improves problem-solving and reflects the customer base.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: A shortcut that estimates how many years an investment takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays reward a competitor who can tell a client on the spot that 8% doubles their money in about nine years.

terms.definition: A classical four-question procedure for locating the exact point at which two sides disagree: conjecture (did it happen?), definition (what should it be called?), quality (how serious is it?) and policy (what should be done about it?). Arguing at the wrong level is the standard failure - answering 'what should we do' while the other side is still disputing whether anything happened produces two speeches that never touch.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge in a conflict roleplay disputes your facts and you answer with a solution, you lose points for never meeting the objection; this names the level you skipped.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: The moral dimension of a decision dropping out of the frame so it gets processed as a budget, legal or scheduling problem instead. The failure is not a person choosing wrong but a person never seeing a choice, which is why euphemism -- 'aggressive accounting', 'creative sourcing' -- is a diagnostic symptom rather than a cosmetic one. It also explains the prediction gap: in one study most participants said they would refuse or confront an improper interview question, and essentially none did when it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making cases are built on decisions already reframed as operational, and the scoring move is to restore the moral question out loud before analyzing the numbers; competitors who answer only the financial framing lose the ethics indicator entirely.

terms.definition: A grid whose rows are performance ratings and whose columns are quartiles of the pay range, with a percentage in each cell: an outstanding performer in the first quartile might receive 6% while the same rating in the fourth quartile receives 3%, and a below-standard rating receives 0% anywhere. The two-way design keeps high performers moving toward the midpoint while stopping anyone from being pushed past the maximum.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a rating and a compa-ratio in a roleplay, you are expected to read the correct cell and explain why two people with the same rating get different percentages.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
