terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Overestimating how much observers notice and later recall one's appearance and actions. Wearers of an embarrassing shirt guessed about half the room could identify it; roughly a quarter could. Unlike the illusion of transparency, the misjudgment is about what is visible on the outside -- a stumble, a stain, an awkward entrance -- rather than about the feelings underneath, and the two are tested as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: Fumbling the first line of a roleplay opener feels catastrophic and costs almost nothing on a judge's rubric; competitors who know the size of the gap recover in one sentence instead of carrying the mistake through the remaining nine minutes.

terms.definition: Employer benefit and payroll-tax cost expressed as a percentage of base pay — $19,500 of insurance, retirement and taxes on a $65,000 salary is a 30% load, making the fully loaded cost $84,500. National figures put benefits near 31% of total compensation, which is why an offer decision compares loaded cost rather than salary alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Budgeting a new position in a roleplay is wrong if you quote only the salary; judges look for the loaded figure when the owner asks what the hire really costs.

terms.definition: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by 365 — the same relationship as inventory turnover but expressed as days on hand, so it falls when turnover rises and 365 divided by turnover reproduces it.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a balance sheet and a cost of goods sold figure, exam questions ask how long a firm's stock sits before selling; answering with the turnover ratio when the item asked for days is a scored miss.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: The proposed tendency to explain one's own behavior by circumstances and another's by disposition. It cannot be treated as a restatement of the fundamental attribution error, and the reason is empirical: a meta-analysis of 173 studies found the overall asymmetry close to zero, surfacing mainly for negative or unexpected events. The honest form of the claim is therefore conditional -- the split appears when something went wrong.
terms.whyItMatters: Bias-recognition items on the Business Administration Core exam use the unqualified version as a distractor, and a roleplay about a missed deadline is scored on asking what got in the way before assigning a trait, because that is exactly the case where the asymmetry does show up.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: Managing the relationship between employers and employees, including unions and disputes.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective labor relations minimize conflict and keep the workforce productive.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: A capability that passes the Prahalad-and-Hamel three-part test — it opens access to multiple markets, contributes visibly to perceived customer benefit, and is hard for rivals to imitate; a strength failing any one of the three is merely a capability and not a basis for strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items list four company strengths and ask which qualifies as a core competency, and the wrong answers are strengths that fail exactly one leg of the test.

terms.definition: Having just done or displayed something creditable makes the next questionable act easier, because the earlier one buys credit against the self-image. It runs opposite to the intuition that good behavior predicts more good behavior: participants who first endorsed a minority candidate afterward favored a white applicant more readily than participants given no chance to establish credentials, so the good act enabled the biased one.
terms.whyItMatters: In an ethics case where a firm cites its diversity award or its donation record while defending a questionable decision, naming the licensing pattern turns a weak 'that is irrelevant' into the analysis a judge scores; it also warns against recommending a visible ethics gesture as the whole remedy.

terms.definition: A premium paid for working a less desirable schedule, set either as cents per hour or as a percentage — commonly 10% for evenings and 15% for nights, so $20.00 an hour becomes $23.00 on nights. It is not overtime: it is owed for the hours themselves regardless of weekly total, and it must be folded into the regular rate before time-and-a-half is computed, so the overtime hour is $34.50, not $30.00.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll questions test whether the differential enters the regular rate before the overtime multiplier, a step candidates routinely skip.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical syllogism, in which one premise is deliberately left unspoken because the audience already believes it and will supply it themselves. 'We should sponsor the tournament - our customers are all high school families' hides the premise that reaching high school families is worth what the sponsorship costs. The unstated premise is where the argument is strongest with a friendly audience and weakest with a hostile one, because attacking what was never said aloud is easier than attacking what was.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that ask what assumption a memo's recommendation rests on are asking you to recover exactly this missing premise.

terms.definition: Bans unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce, and the deception branch is a three-part test: a representation, omission or practice, likely to mislead a consumer acting reasonably under the circumstances, that is material to the purchase decision. The unfairness branch is separate — substantial consumer injury that is not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits — and neither branch requires proving the seller intended to mislead anyone.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion roleplays about an ad whose fine print reverses the headline are scored on materiality and the reasonable-consumer standard, not on intent.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: Blaming an out-group's failures on what its members are like while writing off its successes as luck, special help or an exception -- and reversing both judgments for one's own group. The individual-level attribution error concerns one person; this is its group-level extension, and it is the specific mechanism by which a stereotype survives meeting a counterexample, since the counterexample gets filed away rather than counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on overcoming stereotypes reward naming the filing-as-exception move, and a Human Resources roleplay about a hiring panel that keeps calling qualified candidates from one school 'unusual for their program' is describing this error rather than open prejudice.

terms.definition: An employer contribution formula that exempts a retirement plan from annual nondiscrimination testing: the basic version matches 100% of the first 3% of pay an employee defers plus 50% of the next 2%, capping the employer at 4% of pay, and the alternative is a 3% nonelective contribution to every eligible employee whether they defer or not. Safe harbor money must be fully vested immediately, unlike a discretionary match.
terms.whyItMatters: A benefits roleplay for a small business with highly paid owners turns on the safe harbor as the way to let owners defer fully, and the judge expects the formula.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: The rate applied to the next dollar earned, which is the top bracket a taxpayer reaches rather than the rate paid on all of their income.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-liability items test whether a raise into a higher bracket taxes the whole salary at the new rate — it does not, only the dollars above the bracket line.

terms.definition: In speech act theory (Austin and Searle), the action a speaker performs in saying something - promising, ordering, warning, refusing - as distinct from the locutionary act, which is the literal words and their sense, and the perlocutionary act, which is the effect actually produced in the hearer. 'It is cold in here' is locutionally a remark about temperature, illocutionarily a request, and perlocutionarily successful only if somebody closes the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A service roleplay in which the customer says 'I have been waiting a while' is scored on whether you answer the request rather than the sentence.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: Overestimating both the intensity and the duration of a future emotional reaction; the duration half alone is the durability bias, and the two named causes are focalism -- attending only to the focal event and not to everything else that will fill the day -- and immune neglect, discounting how quickly one rationalizes an outcome. Lottery winners and people newly paralyzed converge far closer than either group predicts.
terms.whyItMatters: A risk-of-personal-decisions item asking whether a competitor should take a demanding promotion is testing this: the answer that survives is one that weighs the ordinary days after the change, not the peak of the reaction to it.

terms.definition: Analyzing the current workforce and forecasting future talent needs.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures a business has the right people and skills to meet its goals.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: A sentence that does not describe an act but carries it out, so it cannot be true or false - only successful or void: 'I accept your offer,' 'I resign,' 'I hereby order 500 units.' Austin's felicity conditions are what make it stick - the right person, the right circumstances, the right form - which is why a casually typed 'agreed' from an authorized employee can create a binding acceptance while a long email full of enthusiasm creates nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask how a staff member bound the company in a chat message turn on this distinction between describing and doing.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: Ownership of employer retirement contributions earned in slices — commonly 20% after two years of service and 20% each year thereafter, reaching 100% at six years, so an employee leaving at year four keeps 60%. The alternative, cliff vesting, gives 0% until a single date and 100% on it, capped by law at three years for defined contribution plans; employee deferrals are always 100% vested from the first dollar under either schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay what a departing employee takes with them, you must apply the schedule to the years of service instead of assuming the whole account balance.

terms.definition: Auditing a small subset of items on a rotating schedule — high-value class A lines several times a year, class C lines once — so the business keeps operating, in contrast with a full physical count, which prices accuracy by shutting the facility for a wall-to-wall count once a year.
terms.whyItMatters: In a shrink-control roleplay the judge expects you to catch record errors continuously without closing the store, and to explain why the rotating audit finds problems months earlier than the annual shutdown.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Technology that stores and manages employee data and HR processes.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRIS improves efficiency and enables data-driven HR decisions.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Creating uncontested demand by raising and creating buyer-value factors while eliminating and reducing costly ones, so value and cost move together; the contrast is red-ocean competition, which fights for share in a defined industry and forces the value-versus-cost trade-off that generic strategy assumes.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship-flavored management roleplays reward reframing the category instead of undercutting a rival on price, and the judge listens for the value-cost simultaneity.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: The right of a worker leaving an employer with 20 or more employees to keep the group health plan for up to 18 months, extended to 29 months for disability and 36 months for a spouse or dependent after divorce or death. The qualified beneficiary has 60 days to elect and may be charged 102% of the full premium — the employer subsidy ends, which is why the monthly cost often quadruples.
terms.whyItMatters: A separation roleplay is scored on stating the election window and that the former employee now pays the full premium plus the 2% administrative charge.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: A defense to copyright infringement weighed on the four statutory factors of 17 U.S.C. section 107: the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is transformative or commercial; the nature of the copyrighted work; the amount and substantiality of the portion taken; and the effect on the potential market for the original. No factor is decisive and there is no safe word count or percentage, though the market-effect factor usually carries the most weight.
terms.whyItMatters: IP-protection roleplays about quoting a rival's review or reusing its product photo in a comparison ad are argued factor by factor.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: The Affordable Care Act rule that an employer averaging 50 or more full-time-equivalent employees in the prior year must offer minimum essential coverage to at least 95% of full-time employees and their dependents or owe a per-employee penalty. Full time here means 30 hours a week or 130 a month, and coverage is affordable only if the employee's share of self-only premium stays under roughly 9.5% of household income as annually indexed.
terms.whyItMatters: A growing-business roleplay that asks whether hiring the 50th worker changes obligations depends on the FTE count and the 30-hour line, not on the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time.
terms.whyItMatters: The balance sheet is where competitors read financial position and solvency.

terms.definition: A member's assertion that the rules are being broken at this moment - a motion made out of order, debate wandering off the pending question, a vote miscounted. It may interrupt a speaker, requires no second, is not debatable, and is settled by the chair's ruling rather than a vote, though any two members may appeal that ruling to the assembly. It must be timely: raised after the offending action is complete, it is normally too late.
terms.whyItMatters: Chapter meetings and management roleplays run on a written agenda test whether you know which objections may interrupt a speaker and which must wait for the floor.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: Offers accepted divided by offers extended, times 100 — 27 acceptances on 36 offers is 75%. Declines by candidates who never received a formal offer are excluded, so the figure isolates whether pay and the closing conversation are competitive, not whether sourcing produced enough applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: In a compensation roleplay, a falling acceptance rate is the evidence that a pay range lags the market; the judge wants the ratio, not an impression that candidates seem unhappy.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: Tufte's format for comparison: a grid of miniature charts sharing identical axes, identical scales and identical design, with exactly one variable changing from panel to panel - one region, one month or one product each. Holding the scale constant across every panel is the whole specification, and letting each panel auto-scale to its own data is the most common way the format is faked, because it destroys the comparison it exists to make.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-visualization task that hands you five years of sales across eight stores is scored on choosing this over one line chart with eight tangled series.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Respecting and adapting to the values and practices of different cultures.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets a business serve diverse markets and build inclusive teams.

terms.definition: The mechanism that ties a state unemployment tax rate to an employer's own history of benefit charges — an employer that has laid off heavily may pay several times the rate of one that has not, on the same taxable wage base. Federal unemployment tax is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, reduced by a 5.4% credit to a net 0.6%, or $42 per employee, when the state account is in good standing.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions about layoffs versus reduced hours turn on the rating consequence, which competitors usually miss by treating unemployment tax as a fixed cost.

terms.definition: The network of people and activities moving a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain thinking underlies inventory, vendor, and cost decisions.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: The highest-ranking class of motion in Robert's Rules - adjourn, recess, raise a question of privilege, call for the orders of the day - urgent enough that it may be made while other business is pending and outranks every subsidiary motion. Because it does not relate to the pending question it is undebatable in most forms, and its rank is exactly why a motion to adjourn can be made while an amendment is on the floor but an amendment cannot be made while adjournment is.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask which motion may be made while another is still pending are testing the precedence ladder, and this class is its top rung.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Maps five ways of handling a disagreement — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating — on two axes: assertiveness, meaning concern for your own outcome, and cooperativeness, meaning concern for the other party's. Collaborating is high on both and costs the most time; compromising sits at the middle of both and splits the difference, so treating those two as synonyms is the classic wrong answer.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict roleplays name a deadline, and the judge wants the mode matched to it — collaborate when the relationship and the outcome both matter and time exists, compromise when it does not.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: A selection interview in which every candidate receives the same predetermined questions in the same order and answers are scored against written anchors, rather than the interviewer following the conversation wherever it goes. Research places its predictive validity near .51 against roughly .38 for the unstructured version, and the fixed script is also what makes the process defensible when a rejected applicant alleges disparate treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay asking how to make interviews fairer is answered by fixing the question set and the scoring key, not by adding a second interviewer.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: A written instruction, issued the moment a company reasonably anticipates a dispute, that suspends every routine deletion schedule and directs named custodians to preserve emails, chat threads, drafts and text messages on the subject. The duty attaches before any complaint is filed, and letting an auto-delete rule keep running past that point is what converts ordinary records management into spoliation, exposing the company to an adverse-inference instruction at trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask what an employee must do with a group chat once a customer threatens to sue are testing this duty and, above all, its trigger point.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: A design in which an employee reports to both a functional manager and a project or product manager at once, trading the single reporting line of a functional structure for cross-unit resource sharing, at the cost of dual-authority conflict and deliberate violation of unity of command.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a staffer pulled between two bosses are scored on identifying the structure by name and proposing a priority-setting mechanism rather than a personality fix.

terms.definition: Divides what is known about a person into four panes by crossing known-to-self against known-to-others: open, blind, hidden and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks the blind pane, while voluntary self-disclosure shrinks the hidden pane — the two moves are not interchangeable, and only the first can surface a habit you cannot see in yourself.
terms.whyItMatters: A written item asking which pane a manager reduces by running a 360-degree review, and roleplays that ask a competitor to assess personal strengths and weaknesses, both depend on separating feedback from disclosure.

terms.definition: Requires equal pay for men and women performing jobs of equal skill, effort and responsibility under similar working conditions in the same establishment, and unlike a Title VII claim it needs no proof of intent. An employer escapes liability only through one of four defenses — a seniority system, a merit system, a system measuring quantity or quality of production, or any factor other than sex — and may never correct a gap by lowering the higher-paid worker's wage.
terms.whyItMatters: A pay-audit roleplay is scored on naming a permitted defense for the differential rather than asserting that the two jobs simply have different titles.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: The measured luminance relationship between text and the background behind it under the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, expressed from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text - 18 point, or 14 point bold - plus 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics; level AAA raises body text to 7:1. Light grey captions and a pale brand colour on a white slide are the two failures that show up most.
terms.whyItMatters: A written event or presentation judged on accessibility is scored on naming the threshold your deck actually meets, not on asserting that the colours look readable.

terms.definition: The principle that a court follows the reasoning of earlier decisions on the same question, which is what makes American case law predictable enough to plan around. Precedent from a higher court in the same jurisdiction binds; decisions from other jurisdictions are only persuasive; and a court may distinguish a case on its facts or, rarely, overrule its own prior holding.
terms.whyItMatters: Sources-of-law exam items ask why a state trial court must follow its own supreme court but may ignore another state's.
